analysis.one_liner: Funds water and sewer repairs, lead pipe replacement, and school drinking water with a tax on corporations' offshore profits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote; no chamber ever considered it before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a dedicated federal trust fund, filled by taxing the foreign profits of multinational corporations, and spend up to $34.85 billion a year on clean water and drinking water programs. The money would pay for fixing and replacing water pipes, replacing lead service lines, testing water in schools, repairing septic systems, and helping rural and tribal communities build water systems. It would also push water services toward public ownership by allowing federal loan funds to be used to buy private water utilities, even from owners who don't want to sell, and to cancel private operation contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing unaffordable water bills, residents with lead service lines, schools needing water testing and new fountains, rural and tribal communities without reliable water or sewer service, and owners of homes with failing septic systems. State revolving loan funds would get a large, steady infusion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead pipes and high water bills

how_it_helps.text: Creates a trust fund, appropriated up to $34.85 billion a year, with 45 percent going to clean water state revolving funds and 44.5 percent to drinking water state revolving funds [S3].

Requires the EPA to set up a grant program to replace lead service lines with lead-free lines, and another grant program for schools to install or repair water fountains, bottle filling stations, and test drinking water quality [S3].
Establishes grants for homeowners to repair, replace, or upgrade septic tanks and drainage fields, and technical assistance for rural, small municipal, and tribal water systems [S3].

Requires the EPA to study nationwide water affordability, water shutoffs due to unpaid bills, and discriminatory access to water and sewer service, with findings reported to Congress within a year [S3].
Requires states to adopt guidance protecting households facing water service disconnection for unpaid bills and promoting universal access to water and sewer service [S3].

Lets state revolving loan funds be used to buy privately owned water and sewer systems from willing or unwilling sellers and to cancel private operation contracts, and restricts drinking water loan funds to publicly owned community water systems [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations, whose foreign subsidiary income would become taxable (no longer tax-deferred) to fill the fund. Private water utilities and private operators of public water systems could also lose business, since federal loan funds could be used to acquire their systems or cancel their contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinational corporations and private water utilities

drawbacks.text: The funding mechanism is a sweeping tax change: it would treat all income of controlled foreign corporations derived from any foreign country as immediately taxable, a major expansion of the taxation of offshore profits whose revenue is estimated rather than guaranteed by the fund's $34.85 billion annual cap [S3].

Allowing purchase of private water systems from 'unwilling sellers' and cancellation of private operation contracts is a forceful shift toward public ownership that opponents would call an unfair taking of existing investments [S3].

The largest shares of the fund flow through existing state revolving loan programs, which historically take years to disburse, so the money would not necessarily reach residents with unaffordable bills or lead pipes quickly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would direct a large, dedicated funding stream at a genuine public need: water systems across the country were aging, and lead contamination and unaffordable water bills were pressing concerns. The main costs fall on multinational corporations and private water operators, not households. The tradeoffs are the aggressiveness of the offshore tax change and the forced-purchase provisions for private water systems, which raise fairness questions even for people sympathetic to the bill's goals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in May 2016, none of which ever held a hearing or acted on it, and Congress ended in January 2017 with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. of Michigan introduced the bill on May 24, 2016, joined by seven original cosponsors [S1].

It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce Committees, and to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, but none of them acted on it [S5].
The bill gathered 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without any vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations avoided the new tax on their offshore profits, and private water utilities avoided being subject to forced purchase; households waiting for lead pipe replacement and water bill relief gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinational firms and private water utilities

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing the water infrastructure trust fund and the tax to fill it.

for.name: 16 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; no member of either party is recorded as opposing it, because the bill never advanced far enough to draw floor opposition.

industries.note: The bill taxes the foreign income of controlled foreign corporations, up to $34.85 billion a year, to fund water infrastructure. Ordinary households would get the infrastructure while the companies bear the bill.

industries.industry: Private water utilities and private water system operators
industries.note: Federal loan funds could be used to buy privately owned water and sewer systems even from unwilling sellers and to cancel private operation contracts, and drinking water loan funds would be limited to publicly owned systems. Households benefit from lower rates; these companies would lose their systems and contracts.

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction and engineering firms
industries.note: A large dedicated fund for pipe replacement, septic repair, and system upgrades would generate contracts and jobs. Communities get the work done.
